item.title: UN allows Palestinian president to again speak via video after US denies visa
item.description: The resolution received 152 votes in favor and three votes against, while four countries abstained.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The United Nations General Assembly voted on Thursday to allow Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas to address the annual gathering of world leaders next week via video - for the second year in a row - after the United States again [USN:FWN4580MT TEXT:"denied"] him a visa to travel to New York. The resolution received 152 votes in favor and three votes against, while four countries abstained. It also allows Abbas and any other high-level Palestinian officials to take part in U.N. meetings or conferences via video over the next year if they are prevented from traveling to the United States. The US said last year that Abbas and about 80 other Palestinians would be affected by its decision to deny and revoke visas from members of the umbrella Palestine Liberation Organization and the West Bank-based Palestinian Authority. Washington announced on Wednesday that it had extended the visa bans. "If the PA wants to be treated as a partner, it must stop subsidizing terror and stop using diplomatic theater as a substitute for serious governance," Deputy US Ambassador to the United Nations Tammy Bruce told the assembly before the vote. Palestinian leaders rejected and condemned the move by the United States, Palestinian UN envoy Riyad Mansour told the General Assembly. Without naming specific officials, the US State Department said on Wednesday it would extend visa sanctions against Palestinian officials over actions they took to "internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian conflict," including pursuing cases against Israel at international tribunals. A Palestinian official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, confirmed Abbas' visa had been denied. Under a 1947 U.N. "headquarters agreement," the U.S. is generally required to allow access for foreign diplomats to the UN in New York. However, Washington has said it can deny visas for security, extremism and foreign policy reasons.

item.title: US to allow Iranian leaders to attend UN General Assembly
item.description: In the past, the US government has barred Iran's delegation from shops and restricted its movements to travel between UN headquarters, the Iranian UN mission and UN ambassador's residence and New York's JFK Airport.
item.dc:creator: Simon Lewis
item.content:encoded: The Trump administration will allow top Iranian officials to attend the United Nations General Assembly in New York next week, the State Department said on Thursday, even as Washington and Tehran remain at war and continue intermittent talks aimed at ending the conflict. A State Department spokesperson said a "core delegation from the Iranian regime" would be allowed to attend the meeting in line with the United States' obligations as the world body's host country. That means officials including Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi will be granted visas, according to a source familiar with the decision. President Donald Trump's administration has held on-again, off-again talks with Iran's leaders aimed at ending the war that began on February 28 when the US and Israel attacked Iran. Tehran responded with strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host US bases. "The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our policy. The delegation is smaller than last year," the State Department spokesperson added. In the past, the US government has [USN:L5N3V91M8 TEXT:"barred "]Iran's delegation from shops and restricted its movements to travel between the United Nations headquarters, the Iranian UN mission and UN ambassador's residence and New York's John F Kennedy Airport. Iran's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment. Under the 1947 U.N. "headquarters agreement," the United States is generally required to allow access to the United Nations for foreign diplomats. But Washington says it can deny visas for "security, terrorism and foreign policy" reasons. The Trump administration on Wednesday said it would [USN:FWN4580MT TEXT:"deny entry to Palestinian officials"] for the UN meeting, extending a ban in place since last year, over actions they took to "internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian conflict," including pursuing cases against Israel at international tribunals. Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas was denied a visa as part of the US move, a Palestinian official said.

item.title: Old photos used to push false claim of 200,000-strong march in Dublin
item.description: Two photos of protests more than a year ago in Ireland have been shared online to misleadingly suggest that they evidence a baseless claim that hundreds of thousands of people marched in Dublin last week during five days of a so-called “total nationwide shutdown”.
item.dc:creator: Reuters Fact Check
item.content:encoded: Two photos of protests more than a year ago in Ireland have been shared online to misleadingly suggest that they evidence a baseless claim that hundreds of thousands of people marched in Dublin last week during five days of a so-called “total nationwide shutdown”. The photo posts said the Irish military was on standby as 200,000 people marched “on Parliament”, while truckers blocked highways. There is no evidence that Ireland endured a five-day national shutdown in early September, nor any credible reporting that 3.6% of Ireland’s 5.5 million population marched through the capital to the Oireachtas. Ireland’s police , An Garda Siochana, said to Reuters in an email that no public gatherings of the type and scale described in the posts have taken place this month or in recent times. The Irish Defence Forces said to Reuters they could only provide support to police by way of formal request and that no such request referencing the online claims had been made. The two photos included in the posts are both more than a year old. Getty Images, crediting photographer Charles McQuillan , published the first photo on April 26, 2025, with a caption saying it showed activists at an anti-immigration rally in Dublin. Getty Images said in an email to Reuters that its caption is accurate. McQuillan said in an email to Reuters that the caption on the Getty Images website lists the correct date. The second photo was published online in September 2024 by Irish photo agency Rollingnews.ie and credited to local photographer Alan Rowlette . The second photo shows anti-immigrant protesters marching in Dublin, according to the agency’s photo caption. Rollingnews.ie said to Reuters that the date printed in its caption is accurate. Rowlette did not respond to a request for comment. Verdict: Miscaptioned. The two photos were captured more than a year ago. There is no evidence that Ireland had a five-day nationwide shutdown in early September, nor that 200,000 people marched through Dublin at that time. (This article was updated on September 18, 2026, to add Charles McQuillan's comment in paragraph 9) This article was produced by the Reuters Fact Check team. Read more  about our fact-checking work.
